translations.literal: Tracing his merit and effect, he suffices to enjoy high noble rank.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Yu's service merited the highest rank,

sentences.zh: 而海內未喻其狀，所受不侔其功，

translations.literal: Yet within the seas have not understood his condition; what he receives does not match his merit,
translations.idiomatic: yet the realm did not grasp his worth and his fief did not match his deeds,

sentences.zh: 〈侔，等也。〉

translations.literal: Mou means equal.
translations.idiomatic: mou meaning equal,

sentences.zh: 臣誠惜之。

translations.literal: your servant truly pities it.
translations.idiomatic: which Cao Cao regretted,

sentences.zh: 乞重平議，增疇戶邑。」

translations.literal: beg to reopen deliberation, increase his equalized household fief.
translations.idiomatic: and asked the court to enlarge his fief accordingly,

sentences.zh: 〈《前書》曰：「復其後代，疇其爵邑。

translations.literal: The Former Documents says: Restore his posterity, equalize his noble fief.
translations.idiomatic: the Former Han formula on matching heirs to founders' fiefs,

sentences.zh: 」音義曰：「疇，等也，使其後常與先人等也。」〉

translations.literal: Pronunciation meaning says: Chou means equal; make his posterity always equal to the former men.
translations.idiomatic: with chou glossed as equalizing posterity with the founders,

sentences.zh: 彧深辭讓。

translations.literal: Yu deeply declined and yielded.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Yu firmly declined,

sentences.zh: 操譬之曰：「昔介子推有言：『竊人之財，猶謂之盜。』

translations.literal: Cao paralleled, saying: In old days Jie Zitui had a saying: To steal another's wealth is still called theft.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao quoted Jie Zitui that taking another's credit is theft,

sentences.zh: 〈《左傳》介子推，晉文公臣。〉

translations.literal: The Zuo Tradition: Jie Zitui, minister of Duke Wen of Jin.
translations.idiomatic: Jie Zitui being a minister of Duke Wen of Jin in the Zuo Tradition,

sentences.zh: 況君竒謨拔出，興亡所係，可專有之邪？

translations.literal: How much more your lord's strange stratagem standing out, on which rise and fall hang—can you monopolize it?
translations.idiomatic: and asked how Xun Yu could monopolize credit for plans on which survival hung,

sentences.zh: 〈操不專功，欲分之於彧也。〉

translations.literal: Cao did not monopolize merit; wished to divide it with Yu.
translations.idiomatic: meaning Cao refused to hoard the glory,

sentences.zh: 雖慕魯連冲高之迹，

translations.literal: Though you admire Lu Zhonglian's lofty-withdrawal traces,
translations.idiomatic: Though Xun Yu admired Lu Zhonglian's refusal of reward,

sentences.zh: 〈《史記》曰，趙欲尊秦爲帝，魯連止之，平原君乃欲封魯連。

translations.literal: The Records says: Zhao wished to honor Qin as emperor; Lu Lian stopped it; Lord Pingyuan then wished to enfeoff Lu Lian.
translations.idiomatic: the Records tale of Lu Lian refusing a fief from Lord Pingyuan,

sentences.zh: 連笑曰：「所貴於天下之士，爲人排患釋難解紛而無取也。

translations.literal: Lian laughed, saying: What is prized in knights of the realm is to remove trouble and undo difficulty and untangle strife without taking reward.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Lian's laugh that a gentleman untangles strife without pay,

sentences.zh: 即有取者，是商賈之士也，而連不忍爲也。」〉

translations.literal: If there is taking, that is the knight of merchants—and Lian cannot bear to do it.
translations.idiomatic: and would not act the merchant,

sentences.zh: 將爲聖人達節之義乎！」

translations.literal: Will you act the sage's doctrine of comprehending the season!
translations.idiomatic: urging him to accept the sage's flexible standard,

sentences.zh: 〈《左傳》曰：「聖達節，次守節。」〉

translations.literal: The Zuo Tradition says: Sages comprehend the season; next guard the season.
translations.idiomatic: from the Zuo Tradition on sages and timing,

sentences.zh: 於是增封千戶，并前二千戶。

translations.literal: Thereupon added enfeoffment one thousand households, together with before two thousand households.
translations.idiomatic: so his fief rose by a thousand households to two thousand in all.

sentences.zh: 又欲授以正司，

translations.literal: Again wished to confer on him the regular office,
translations.idiomatic: The court again meant to give him a formal appointment to the post,

sentences.zh: 〈彧先守尚書令，今欲正除也。〉

translations.literal: Note: Yu had first been acting guardian director of the secretariat; now they wished to appoint him to the substantive post.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Xun Yu had been serving as acting director of the secretariat; the plan was now to confirm him in the full title.

sentences.zh: 彧使荀攸深自陳讓，至于十數，乃止。

translations.literal: Yu had Xun You press his declinations earnestly, reaching to a dozen or more times, and then it stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Yu sent Xun You to press his repeated refusals—more than ten times—before the matter was dropped.

sentences.zh: 操將伐劉表，問彧所策。

translations.literal: Cao was about to attack Liu Biao and asked Yu what strategy to take.
translations.idiomatic: When Cao Cao was preparing to strike Liu Biao, he asked Xun Yu for a plan.

sentences.zh: 彧曰：「今華夏以平，荊、漢知亡矣，可聲出宛、葉而閒行輕進，以掩其不意。

translations.literal: Yu said: Now the central lands are already pacified; Jing and the Han region know they are doomed. You may make a show of marching out through Wan and Ye while sending a light column by secret routes to strike where they do not expect.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Yu said, “The heartland is already settled; the Jing–Han region knows it is finished. Feint a thrust through Wan and Ye, then slip a fast, light force along byways to catch them off guard.”

sentences.zh: 」操從之。

translations.literal: Cao followed this.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao adopted the advice.

sentences.zh: 會表病死。

translations.literal: It happened that Biao fell ill and died.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Biao then fell ill and died.

sentences.zh: 〈《魏志》，操如彧計，表子琮以州逆降。〉

translations.literal: The Wei Records states: Cao followed Yu’s plan, and Biao’s son Cong surrendered the province in submission.
translations.idiomatic: The Wei Records notes that Cao Cao followed Xun Yu’s design and that Liu Biao’s son Liu Cong yielded the province in surrender.

sentences.zh: 十七年，董昭等

translations.literal: In the seventeenth year, Dong Zhao and others
translations.idiomatic: In the seventeenth year of the Jian’an era, Dong Zhao and others

sentences.zh: 〈昭字公仁，濟陰人也。〉

translations.literal: Note: Zhao, courtesy name Gongren, was a man of Jiyin.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Dong Zhao, styled Gongren, came from Jiyin.

sentences.zh: 欲共進操爵國公，九錫備物，

translations.literal: wished jointly to advance Cao’s noble rank to duke of a state and to complete the nine bestowals and their full paraphernalia,
translations.idiomatic: They sought jointly to raise Cao Cao to the rank of duke of a state and to award him the full regalia of the nine bestowals,

sentences.zh: 〈禮含文嘉曰：「九錫一曰車馬，二曰衣服，三曰樂器，四曰朱戶，五曰納陛，六曰虎賁百人，七曰斧鉞，八曰弓矢，九曰秬鬯，謂之九錫。

translations.literal: The Rites, Hanwenjia chapter, says: The nine bestowals are, first, chariots and horses; second, robes; third, musical instruments; fourth, vermilion doors; fifth, the stepped ascent; sixth, a hundred tiger guards; seventh, axe and halberd; eighth, bow and arrows; ninth, black millet ale—these are called the nine bestowals.
translations.idiomatic: The ritual text Hanwenjia lists the nine bestowals: chariots and horses; robes; instruments; vermilion doors; the palace stair; a hundred tiger guards; the axe and halberd; bow and arrows; and the dark-millet ale—the nine gifts so named.

sentences.zh: 錫，與也，九錫皆如其德。

translations.literal: Xi means ‘to give’; each of the nine bestowals matches his virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Xi means ‘to grant,’ and each of the nine honors was meant to match the recipient’s virtue.

sentences.zh: 」《左傳》曰：「分魯公以大路大旂，夏后氏之璜，封父之繁弱，祝宗卜史，備物典策。」〉

translations.literal: The Zuo Tradition says: They divided to the duke of Lu the great chariot and great banner, the Xia hou’s jade, Fengfu’s bow, invocators, lineage masters, diviners, and scribes—complete paraphernalia and canonical documents. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: The Zuo Tradition adds that the duke of Lu received the great chariot and banner, the jade of the Xia, the Fengfu bow, ritual officers, and full ceremonial gear and records. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 密以訪彧。

translations.literal: Secretly consulted Yu about it.
translations.idiomatic: They sounded Xun Yu out on the plan in private.

sentences.zh: 彧曰「曹公本興義兵，以匡振漢朝，雖勳庸崇著，猶秉忠貞之節。

translations.literal: Yu said: Lord Cao originally raised a righteous host to rescue and restore the Han house; though his merit and achievements tower high, he still holds to loyal and steadfast integrity.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Yu said, “Lord Cao first took up arms in a righteous cause to set the Han to rights. However great his merit, he has kept faith with the dynasty.”

sentences.zh: 君子愛人以德，不宜如此。

translations.literal: A gentleman loves others by nurturing their virtue; it is not fitting to do thus.
translations.idiomatic: A gentleman serves another’s good by moral means; this is not the way to treat him.”

sentences.zh: 」事遂寑。

translations.literal: The matter then was shelved.
translations.idiomatic: The proposal was shelved.

sentences.zh: 〈《禮記》曰「君子之愛人也以德，細人之愛人也以姑息」也。〉

translations.literal: The Record of Rites says: The gentleman’s love for others is by virtue; the petty man’s love for others is by indulgence.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: The Record of Rites contrasts the gentleman’s love, which builds character, with the small man’s, which is mere indulgence.

sentences.zh: 操心不能平。

translations.literal: Cao’s heart could not be calmed.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao could not set the slight aside.

sentences.zh: 會南征孫權，表請彧勞軍于譙，因表留彧曰：「臣聞古之遣將，上設監督之重，下建副二之任，

translations.literal: When he was about to campaign south against Sun Quan, he memorialized asking Yu to review the army at Qiao, and by memorial sought to detain Yu, saying: I have heard that in antiquity when sending forth generals, above they set the weight of overseers; below they established the duty of seconds,
translations.idiomatic: On the southern expedition against Sun Quan, Cao Cao memorialized that Xun Yu should review the troops at Qiao, then used a second memorial to keep him there: “Ancient custom placed heavy overseers above a field commander and paired seconds below him,

sentences.zh: 〈《史記》，齊景公以田穰苴爲將軍，扞燕。

translations.literal: The Records states: Duke Jing of Qi made Tian Rangju general to resist Yan.
translations.idiomatic: The Records tells how Duke Jing of Qi named Tian Rangju general against Yan.

sentences.zh: 苴曰：「臣素卑賤，擢之閭伍之中，加之大夫之上，士卒未附，百姓不信，權輕，願得君之寵臣，國之所尊，以監軍，乃可。

translations.literal: Rangju said: I have always been base and lowly; raised from the lanes and squads and set above great officers, the troops are not yet attached and the people do not trust me; my authority is light. I wish to obtain one of your favored ministers, whom the state esteems, to oversee the army—only then may it be done.
translations.idiomatic: Rangju replied, “I am of mean origin, pulled from the ranks above senior officers; the soldiers do not yet follow me, and the people do not trust my light authority. Give me one of your trusted ministers, honored in the state, to supervise the host, and it can be done.”

sentences.zh: 」景公許之，使莊賈往。

translations.literal: Duke Jing granted it and sent Zhuang Jia to go.
translations.idiomatic: The duke agreed and sent Zhuang Jia.

sentences.zh: 即監督之義也。〉

translations.literal: This is the meaning of overseer. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: That is the sense of “overseer” intended here. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 所以尊嚴國命，謀而鮮過者也。

translations.literal: by which the dignity of the state’s command is upheld and plans seldom go wrong.
translations.idiomatic: Thus the majesty of the state’s orders is upheld and counsel rarely errs.

sentences.zh: 〈《左傳》曰：「謀而鮮過，惠訓不倦。」〉

translations.literal: The Zuo Tradition says: In planning seldom erring, in kindly instruction never weary.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: The Zuo Tradition praises counsel that seldom fails and teaching that never tires.

sentences.zh: 臣今當濟江，奉辭伐罪，宜有大使肅將王命。

translations.literal: Your servant now must cross the Yangzi, bearing the charge to punish the guilty; there ought to be a great envoy solemnly bearing the king’s command.
translations.idiomatic: I am about to cross the river on a punitive mission; a senior envoy should carry the imperial charge with fitting gravity.”

sentences.zh: 文武並用，自古有之。

translations.literal: Civil and military used together—since antiquity there has been this.
translations.idiomatic: Civil and military means have always been paired.”

sentences.zh: 使持節侍中守尚書令萬歲亭侯彧，國之望臣，德洽華夏，旣停軍所次，便宜與臣俱進，宣示國命，威懷醜虜。

translations.literal: The commissioner bearing credentials, palace attendant, acting guardian director of the secretariat, Marquis of Wansui Precinct, Yu, is a minister on whom the state’s hopes rest; his virtue spreads through the central lands. Since he has halted where the army camps, it is fitting that he advance together with your servant, proclaiming the state’s command and overawing and winning the enemy.
translations.idiomatic: The commissioner with insignia, palace attendant, acting director of the secretariat, and Marquis of Wansui Precinct, Xun Yu, is a pillar of the state whose virtue runs through the realm. As he has paused where the army rests, he should march with me to proclaim the court’s will and overawe the foe.”

sentences.zh: 軍禮尚速，不及先請，臣輒留彧，依以爲重。

translations.literal: Military ritual esteems speed; there was no time to request beforehand; your servant therefore detained Yu, relying on him for weight.
translations.idiomatic: Field etiquette prizes speed, so I could not wait for prior approval; I have therefore kept Xun Yu with the army as my mainstay.”

sentences.zh: 」書奏，帝從之，遂以彧爲侍中、光祿大夫，持節，參丞相軍事。

translations.literal: When the memorial was presented, the emperor followed it, and Yu was then made palace attendant, grand master of splendid happiness, bearer of credentials, and participant in the chancellor’s military affairs.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor approved the memorial, and Xun Yu was appointed palace attendant, grand master of splendid happiness, credential-bearer, and adviser on the chancellor’s staff.

sentences.zh: 至濡須，

translations.literal: When they reached Ruxu,
translations.idiomatic: When the host reached Ruxu,

sentences.zh: 〈濡須，水名也，在今和州歷陽縣西南。

translations.literal: Note: Ruxu is the name of a water, now southwest of Liyang County in Hezhou.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Ruxu is a river name, southwest of present-day Liyang in Hezhou.

sentences.zh: 吳錄曰：「孫權聞操來，夾水立塢，狀如偃月，以相拒，月餘乃退。」〉

translations.literal: The Wu Record says: When Sun Quan heard Cao was coming, he built stockades along both banks in the shape of a reclining moon to oppose him; after more than a month Cao withdrew. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: The Wu Record says Sun Quan threw up crescent-shaped ramparts along the river to hold Cao Cao off for over a month before he withdrew. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 彧病留壽春，

translations.literal: Yu fell ill and remained at Shouchun,
translations.idiomatic: Xun Yu fell ill and was left at Shouchun,

sentences.zh: 〈壽春，縣，屬淮南郡，今壽州郡也。〉

translations.literal: Note: Shouchun is a county belonging to Huainan commandery; it is now Shouzhou commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Shouchun county lay in Huainan commandery, in what is now Shouzhou.

sentences.zh: 操饋之食，發視，乃空器也，於是飲藥而卒。

translations.literal: Cao sent him food; when he opened and looked, it was an empty vessel; thereupon he drank poison and died.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao sent a meal; when the cover was lifted, the vessels were empty. Xun Yu took poison and died.

sentences.zh: 時年五十。

translations.literal: At the time he was fifty sui.
translations.idiomatic: He was fifty years old.

sentences.zh: 〈《獻帝春秋》，董承之誅，伏后與父完書，言司空殺董承，帝方爲報怨。

translations.literal: The Annals of Emperor Xian: At Dong Cheng’s execution, Empress Fu wrote to her father Wan, saying the minister of works had killed Dong Cheng and the emperor was then seeking revenge.
translations.idiomatic: The Annals of Emperor Xian relates that after Dong Cheng’s death, Empress Fu wrote her father Fu Wan that the minister of works had executed Dong Cheng while the emperor still nursed a grievance.

sentences.zh: 完得書以示彧，彧惡之，隱而不言。

translations.literal: When Wan received the letter he showed it to Yu; Yu detested it and concealed it without speaking.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Wan showed the letter to Xun Yu, who was appalled and kept silent.

sentences.zh: 完以示其妻弟樊普，普封以呈太祖，太祖陰爲之備。

translations.literal: Wan showed it to his wife’s younger brother Fan Pu; Pu sealed and presented it to the Grand Progenitor, who secretly made preparations on account of it.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Wan also showed it to his brother-in-law Fan Pu, who sealed it and sent it to Cao Cao, who quietly laid his plans.

sentences.zh: 彧恐事覺，欲自發之，因求使至鄴，勸太祖以女配帝。

translations.literal: Yu feared the affair would be discovered and wished to expose it himself; therefore he sought mission to Ye and urged the Grand Progenitor to give a daughter to the emperor as consort.
translations.idiomatic: Fearing exposure, Xun Yu tried to get ahead of the plot by asking leave to go to Ye and urging Cao Cao to marry a daughter into the palace.

sentences.zh: 太祖曰：「今朝廷有伏后，吾女何得配上？

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor said: Now the court has Empress Fu; how could my daughter be matched to the throne?
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao replied, “The court already has Empress Fu; how can my daughter enter the harem?”

sentences.zh: 」彧曰：「伏后無子，性又凶邪，往甞與父書，言詞醜惡，可因此廢也。

translations.literal: Yu said: Empress Fu has no sons; her nature is moreover cruel and depraved; in the past she once wrote her father with ugly words—on this ground she may be deposed.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Yu said, “The empress is sonless and vicious; she once wrote her father intemperate letters—grounds enough to set her aside.”

sentences.zh: 」太祖曰：「卿昔何不道之？

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor said: Why did you not speak of it in the past?
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao asked, “Why did you never mention this before?”

sentences.zh: 」彧陽驚曰：「昔已甞爲公言也。

translations.literal: Yu feigned surprise and said: In the past I already once spoke to the lord about it.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Yu pretended astonishment: “I did tell you, my lord.”

sentences.zh: 」太祖曰：「此豈小事，而吾忘之！

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor said: How could this be a small matter, and I forget it!
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao said, “A matter of this weight—and I would forget?”

sentences.zh: 」太祖以此恨彧，而外含容之。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor on this account harbored resentment toward Yu, yet outwardly contained him.
translations.idiomatic: From that day Cao Cao nursed a grudge against Xun Yu while still treating him with outward respect.

sentences.zh: 至董昭建魏公議，彧意不同，欲言之於太祖，乃齎璽書犒軍，飲饗禮畢，彧請間，太祖知彧欲言，揖而遣之，遂不得。

translations.literal: When Dong Zhao raised the proposal for the Wei duke, Yu’s mind differed; he wished to speak of it to the Grand Progenitor. Then bearing the imperial document he went to reward the army; when the drinking feast rites were finished, Yu asked for a private audience; the Grand Progenitor knew Yu wished to speak, bowed with hands joined and sent him away, so he could not get through.
translations.idiomatic: When Dong Zhao pressed the motion to ennoble Cao as duke of Wei, Xun Yu disagreed and meant to remonstrate. He carried an edict to feast the army; after the banquet he asked for a private word. Cao Cao guessed his intent, bowed him out, and gave him no chance to speak.

sentences.zh: 留之，卒於壽春。〉

translations.literal: Detained him; he died at Shouchun. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: He was kept there and died at Shouchun. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 帝哀惜之，祖日爲之廢讌樂。

translations.literal: The emperor mourned and pitied him; on the ancestral day for him he suspended feasting and music.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor grieved for him and canceled banquet music on the ancestral day observed in his honor.

sentences.zh: 〈祖日謂祭祖神之日，因爲讌樂也。

translations.literal: Note: Ancestral day means the day of sacrificing to the ancestral spirit; on it there was feasting and music.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: “Ancestral day” was the feast honoring the patron spirit of travel,

sentences.zh: 《風俗通》曰：「共工氏子曰脩，好遠遊，祀以爲祖神。

translations.literal: The Comprehensive Meaning of Customs and Usages says: Gonggong’s son was named Xiu; he loved to travel far and was sacrificed to as the ancestral spirit.
translations.idiomatic: and the Comprehensive Meaning of Customs explains that Gonggong’s wandering son Xiu became its tutelary deity.

sentences.zh: 漢以午日祖。」〉

translations.literal: The Han took the wu day for the ancestral rite. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: The Han marked that rite on the wu day of the cycle.” End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 謚曰敬侯。

translations.literal: His posthumous title was reverent marquis.
translations.idiomatic: He was given the posthumous title Reverent Marquis.

sentences.zh: 明年，操遂稱魏公云。

translations.literal: The next year, Cao then styled himself duke of Wei, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: The following year Cao Cao took the title duke of Wei.

sentences.zh: 論曰：自遷帝西京，山東騰沸，

translations.literal: Discussion says: From the time the emperor was moved to the western capital, east of the mountains boiled up,
translations.idiomatic: The historian’s judgment: After the emperor was removed to the western capital, the lands east of the mountains seethed,

sentences.zh: 〈詩曰：「百川沸騰。」〉

translations.literal: The Odes says: The hundred streams boil up.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: The Odes speaks of “the hundred streams boiling over.”

sentences.zh: 天下之命倒縣矣。

translations.literal: The fate of the realm hung inverted.
translations.idiomatic: the fate of the empire hung upside down.

sentences.zh: 〈趙岐注《孟子》曰：「倒縣猶困苦也。」〉

translations.literal: Zhao Qi’s commentary on Mencius says: Inverted hanging is like extreme hardship.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Zhao Qi glosses “inverted” as utter distress.

sentences.zh: 荀君乃越河、兾，間關以從曹氏。

translations.literal: Lord Xun then crossed the Yellow River and Ji, in hardship and twists to follow the Cao house.
translations.idiomatic: Lord Xun Yu crossed the Yellow River and the Ji region, making a hard road of it to join the Caos.

sentences.zh: 〈間關猶展轉也。〉

translations.literal: Note: Jianguan is like turning and tossing.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: “Jianguan” here means a winding, difficult journey.

sentences.zh: 察其定舉措，

translations.literal: Observing his settled measures,
translations.idiomatic: Watching how he set policy,

sentences.zh: 〈措，置也。〉

translations.literal: Note: Cuo means to place.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Cuo means “to set” or “to arrange.”

sentences.zh: 立言策，崇明王略，以急國艱，豈云因亂假義，以就違正之謀乎？

translations.literal: establishing words and plans, exalting and clarifying the kingly strategy, to relieve the state’s peril—how could one say he borrowed righteousness amid chaos to pursue a design that violated the right?
translations.idiomatic: framing counsel and exalting the royal design to ease the dynasty’s peril—can that be dismissed as seizing a moral pretext in turmoil to serve a crooked end?

sentences.zh: 〈言彧本心不背漢也，〉

translations.literal: Note: This says Yu’s original mind did not turn against the Han.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: The point is that Xun Yu’s heart never turned against the Han.

sentences.zh: 誠仁爲己任，期紓民於倉卒也。

translations.literal: Truly he took benevolence as his burden, hoping to relieve the people in sudden crisis.
translations.idiomatic: He truly took humanity as his charge and hoped to spare the people in the crisis of the moment.

sentences.zh: 〈紓，緩也，音舒。〉

translations.literal: Note: Shu means to ease; pronounced like shu.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Shu means “to ease,” read like the character for “relax.”

sentences.zh: 及阻董昭之議，以致非命，豈數也夫！

translations.literal: When he blocked Dong Zhao’s proposal and thereby met an unnatural death—was it fate indeed!
translations.idiomatic: When he blocked Dong Zhao’s scheme and paid with his life, was that mere chance?

sentences.zh: 世言荀君者，通塞或過矣。

translations.literal: What the age says of Lord Xun, on success and obstruction, may sometimes go too far.
translations.idiomatic: Popular talk about Lord Xun Yu—whether he flourished or was blocked—often misses the mark.

sentences.zh: 常以爲中賢以下，道無求備，智筭有所研踈，原始未必要末。

translations.literal: I have always held that below middling worthies one does not demand completeness in the Way; in calculation of wisdom there are places refined or rough; tracing the beginning does not always require matching the end.
translations.idiomatic: Below the middling sage one cannot demand perfection: wit may excel in one place and falter in another, and a noble start need not guarantee the same end.

sentences.zh: 斯理之不可全詰者也。

translations.literal: This is a principle that cannot be exhaustively pressed.
translations.idiomatic: That is a truth no moral audit can exhaust.

sentences.zh: 夫以衞賜之賢，一說而斃兩國。

translations.literal: Now as for the worth of Wei Ci, with one persuasion he brought down two states.
translations.idiomatic: Even Wei Ci’s genius—one round of diplomacy undid two kingdoms.

sentences.zh: 〈兩國謂齊與吳也。

translations.literal: Note: The two states mean Qi and Wu.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: The two states are Qi and Wu.

sentences.zh: 端木賜字子貢，衞人也。

translations.literal: Duanmu Ci, courtesy name Zigong, was a man of Wei.
translations.idiomatic: Duanmu Ci, styled Zigong, was a native of Wei.

sentences.zh: 田常欲伐魯，仲尼令出使勸田常伐吳，常許之。

translations.literal: Tian Chang wished to attack Lu; Zhongni ordered him to go on mission and urge Tian Chang to attack Wu; Chang assented.
translations.idiomatic: When Tian Chang planned to attack Lu, Confucius sent Zigong to persuade him to strike Wu instead, and Tian Chang agreed.

sentences.zh: 賜又至吳，請夫差伐齊。

translations.literal: Ci also went to Wu and asked Fuchai to attack Qi.
translations.idiomatic: Zigong then went to Wu and urged King Fuchai to march against Qi.

sentences.zh: 又之越，說句踐將兵助吳。

translations.literal: Again he went to Yue and persuaded Gou Jian to lead troops to aid Wu.
translations.idiomatic: He next visited Yue and talked Gou Jian into sending troops to help Wu.

sentences.zh: 又之晉，說以兵待吳伐齊之弊。

translations.literal: Again he went to Jin and persuaded them with troops to await the exhaustion of Wu’s attack on Qi.
translations.idiomatic: He then went to Jin and urged it to hold its army ready for the weariness that would follow Wu’s campaign in Qi.

sentences.zh: 吳旣勝齊，與晉爭彊，晉果敗吳，越襲其後，遂殺夫差。

translations.literal: Once Wu had defeated Qi, it contended with Jin for supremacy; Jin indeed defeated Wu, Yue struck from behind, and thereupon killed Fuchai.
translations.idiomatic: Wu beat Qi, then clashed with Jin for dominance; Jin broke Wu’s power, Yue struck from the rear, and Fuchai died.

sentences.zh: 故子貢一出，存魯，亂齊，破吳，彊晉，霸越。〉

translations.literal: Therefore one outing of Zigong preserved Lu, threw Qi into turmoil, broke Wu, strengthened Jin, and made Yue hegemon. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: Thus a single mission preserved Lu, ruined Qi, shattered Wu, bolstered Jin, and crowned Yue. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 彼非薄於仁而欲之，蓋有全必有喪也，斯又功之不兼者也。

translations.literal: It was not that he was shallow in benevolence yet desired it—where there is preservation there must also be loss; this again is where achievements cannot be combined.
translations.idiomatic: That was not because he scanted humanity for gain: every gain costs something else—no single deed can compass every good.

sentences.zh: 〈子貢不欲違仁義而致晉，但其事不兼濟也。

translations.literal: Note: Zigong did not wish to violate benevolence and rightness to bring about Jin, but the affair could not aid all sides.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Zigong did not mean to betray moral duty to elevate Jin, yet one stroke could not save every state.

sentences.zh: 言彧豈願彊曹氏令代漢哉？

translations.literal: This says how could Yu have wished to strengthen the Cao house to replace the Han?
translations.idiomatic: The text asks whether Xun Yu truly wanted to build the Caos into usurpers of the Han.

sentences.zh: 事不得已也。〉

translations.literal: The affair was what could not be helped. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: He was caught in what could not be helped. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 方時運之屯邅，

translations.literal: When the times’ fortune was blocked and halting,
translations.idiomatic: In an age stumbling through hardship,

sentences.zh: 〈《易》曰：「屯如邅如。

translations.literal: The Changes says: Blocked like, halting like.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: The Changes reads, “Blocked and stumbling,”

sentences.zh: 」邅音竹連反。〉

translations.literal: Zhan is pronounced like zhu-lian fan. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: with zhan read in the zhu-lian cut. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 非雄才無以濟其溺，功高埶彊，則皇器自移矣。

translations.literal: Without heroic talent there is no way to save them from drowning; when merit is high and power strong, then the imperial regalia shifts of itself.
translations.idiomatic: Only a heroic talent could pull the realm from the flood; once power towers, the throne slips away on its own.

sentences.zh: 〈謂魏太祖功業大而神器自歸也。〉

translations.literal: Note: This means Wei’s Grand Progenitor’s achievements were great and the sacred vessel returned to him of itself.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Cao Cao’s deeds grew so great that the mandate gravitated to him.

sentences.zh: 此又時之不可並也。

translations.literal: This again is where the times cannot be combined.
translations.idiomatic: That, too, is what the age will not allow to be reconciled.

sentences.zh: 蓋取其歸正而已，亦殺身以成仁之義也。

translations.literal: In general he took returning to the right as enough—it is also the meaning of destroying the body to complete benevolence.
translations.idiomatic: He chose to stand by the right even at the cost of his life—the sense of Confucius’s “die to perfect benevolence.”

translations.literal: Praise section marker.
translations.idiomatic: Section heading: encomium.

sentences.zh: 贊曰：公業稱豪，駿聲升騰。

translations.literal: The encomium says: Gongye was hailed a champion; his splendid name rose aloft.
translations.idiomatic: The encomium runs: Gongye was hailed a hero, and his fair fame climbed high.

sentences.zh: 權詭時偪，

translations.literal: He wielded stratagem when the times pressed,
translations.idiomatic: When crisis pressed, he answered with wiles,

sentences.zh: 〈謂詭辭以對卓。〉

translations.literal: Note: This means he used deceitful words to answer Dong Zhuo.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: He dissembled before Dong Zhuo.

sentences.zh: 揮金僚朋。

translations.literal: scattering gold among colleagues and friends.
translations.idiomatic: He scattered gold among friends and allies.

sentences.zh: 〈揮，散也。〉

translations.literal: Note: Hui means to scatter.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: “Scatter” is the sense of hui here.

sentences.zh: 北海天逸，音情頓挫。

translations.literal: The lord of Beihai was free as heaven; his tones and feeling rose and fell.
translations.idiomatic: The lord of Beihai moved with heaven’s ease, his voice and passion breaking in waves.

sentences.zh: 〈逸，縱也。

translations.literal: Note: Yi means to give free rein.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Here yi means “unrestrained ease.”

sentences.zh: 頓挫猶抑揚也。〉

translations.literal: Duncuo is like rising and falling. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Duncuo means cadence, rise and fall. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 越俗易驚，孤音少和。

translations.literal: Yue customs are easily startled; a lone note seldom finds harmony.
translations.idiomatic: The south startles easily; a solitary voice rarely finds a chorus.

sentences.zh: 直轡安歸，高謀誰佐？

translations.literal: Straight reins—where to return? Lofty plans—who will assist?
translations.idiomatic: The straight road offers no homecoming; whose hand steadies so high a design?

sentences.zh: 〈直轡，直道也。

translations.literal: Note: Straight reins means the straight path.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: “Straight reins” stands for the upright way.

sentences.zh: 言其道無所歸，謀謨之高欲誰佐也。〉

translations.literal: It says his way had nowhere to return, and who would second so lofty a design. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: It means he had no safe road back, and no ally for his grand counsel. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 彧之有弼，誠感國疾。

translations.literal: In Yu’s having a helper, truly he felt the state’s sickness.
translations.idiomatic: That Xun Yu had a counterpart shows how keenly he felt the dynasty’s ailment.

sentences.zh: 功申運改，迹疑心一。

translations.literal: Merit extended, fortune changed; tracks seemed doubtful, yet the heart was one.
translations.idiomatic: Times shifted and deeds ran on; the record looks tangled, but the purpose never wavered.

sentences.zh: 〈迹若可疑，心如一心。〉

translations.literal: Note: The tracks seem doubtful, yet the heart is single-minded. Closing note.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary: Outward signs may puzzle, inward resolve did not. End of gloss.

sentences.zh: 校勘記

translations.literal: Collation notes.
translations.idiomatic: Textual collation notes.

sentences.zh: 二二五七頁三行司農觿之曾孫也按：「曾孫」當作「玄孫」。

translations.literal: Page 2257, line 3, Minister of Agriculture Xi’s great-grandson—note: “great-grandson” should read “great-great-grandson.”
translations.idiomatic: Collation: for “great-grandson of Minister Xi,” read “fifth-generation descendant (玄孫).”

sentences.zh: 泰弟渾，魏志有傳，雲高祖父觿，則泰乃觿之玄孫也。

translations.literal: Tai’s younger brother Hun has a biography in the Wei Records; it says his remote grandfather was Xi, so Tai is actually Xi’s great-great-grandson.
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Hun’s Wei biography names Xi as a remote ancestor, so Zheng Tai is Xi’s fifth-generation descendant, not merely a great-grandson.

sentences.zh: 二二五八頁一一行將各*

translations.literal: Page 2258, line 11: jiang ge [lacuna]*
translations.idiomatic: Page 2258, line 11: the phrase “each general …” is damaged in the print.

translations.literal: (ji / base)
translations.idiomatic: Alternate reading supplied: ji (“base”).

sentences.zh: **[潟]*峙刊誤謂案文「基」當作「潟」，謂如潟不動。

translations.literal: **[xi]* zhi: Kanwu says the text’s ji should read xi, meaning “still as a salt marsh.”
translations.idiomatic: The collation argues ji should be xi (still water), not “base.”

sentences.zh: 按：王先謙謂魏志鄭渾傳注引張璠漢紀作「潟峙」。

translations.literal: Note: Wang Xianqian says the Wei Records, Zheng Hun commentary citing Zhang Fan’s Han Annals, has “xi zhi.”
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xianqian cites the Zhang Fan Han Annals parallel with xi zhi.

sentences.zh: 今據改。

translations.literal: Now emended accordingly.
translations.idiomatic: The text is emended accordingly.

sentences.zh: 二二五八頁一二行婦女猶戴戟操矛按：王先謙謂戟不能戴，魏志鄭渾傳注引張璠漢紀作「載戟」。

translations.literal: Page 2258, line 12: women still dai ji and wield spears—note: Wang Xianqian says halberds cannot be dai; the Wei commentary cites Zhang Fan’s Han Annals as zai ji (“carry halberds”).
translations.idiomatic: Collation: dai ji should be zai ji—“bearing halberds”—per Wang Xianqian and the Wei commentary.

sentences.zh: 二二五八頁一三行百姓所畏者有並涼之人按：刊誤謂案文多一「有」字。

translations.literal: Page 2258, line 13: what the common people fear are persons from Bing and Liang—note: Kanwu says the text has an extra you (“have”).
translations.idiomatic: Collation: delete the stray you before “people from Bing and Liang.”

sentences.zh: 二二五九頁一五行說菀曰汲本、殿本「菀」作「苑」。

translations.literal: Page 2259, line 15: speaks to Wan yue—Jizhou and Palace editions write yuan for wan.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: wan / yuan variant in “speaks to the park.”

sentences.zh: 按：菀苑通。

translations.literal: Note: wan and yuan are interchangeable here.
translations.idiomatic: Wan and yuan are equivalent graphs in this context.

sentences.zh: 二二五九頁一五行聲響動天按：「響」原斗「向」，逕改正。

translations.literal: Page 2259, line 15: sound and echo shake heaven—note: xiang “echo” was miswritten as xiang “direction”; corrected directly.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: the echo character 響 was mis-copied as 向 and is corrected.

sentences.zh: 二二六０頁一０行景帝*

translations.literal: Page 2260, line 10: Emperor Jing*
translations.idiomatic: Page 2260, line 10: the reign year for Emperor Jing is damaged.

translations.literal: (two)
translations.idiomatic: The numeral supplied is “two.”

sentences.zh: **[三]*年反據殿本改。

translations.literal: **[three]* years rebel—emended per the Palace edition.
translations.idiomatic: Read “third year” of the revolt, following the Palace edition.

sentences.zh: 二二六０頁一四行年四十一汲本、殿本作「四十二」。

translations.literal: Page 2260, line 14: age forty-one—Jizhou and Palace editions read forty-two.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: age forty-one versus forty-two in the editions.

sentences.zh: 按：魏志鄭渾傳注作「四十一」，盧弼校雲宋本作「四十二」。

translations.literal: Note: The Wei Records, Zheng Hun commentary, has forty-one; Lu Bi’s collation says the Song edition reads forty-two.
translations.idiomatic: The Wei commentary has forty-one; Lu Bi notes the Song text prefers forty-two.

sentences.zh: 二二六一頁三行霸字次*

translations.literal: Page 2261, line 3: Ba’s courtesy name ci*
translations.idiomatic: Page 2261, line 3: Yan Ba’s courtesy name is partly lost.

translations.literal: (ru / child)
translations.idiomatic: Alternate reading: ru (“child”).

sentences.zh: **[儒]*據汲本、殿本改，與前書合。

translations.literal: **[ru]*: emended per Jizhou and Palace editions to agree with the Former Han.
translations.idiomatic: Emended to ru to match the Former Han parallel.

sentences.zh: 二二六一頁七行太中大夫陳煒按：袁紀「煒」作「禕」。

translations.literal: Page 2261, line 7: Grand counselor Chen wei—note: Yuan ji writes yi for wei.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: Chen Wei vs Chen Yi in the Yuan Annals.

sentences.zh: 二二六一頁九行將不早惠乎殿本「惠」作「慧」，冊府元龜七七三卷同。

translations.literal: Page 2261, line 9: will you not be early hui—Palace edition writes hui “clever”; Cefu yuangui 773 agrees.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: the Palace text and Cefu yuangui write hui “clever” for hui “kind.”

sentences.zh: 按：惠慧通。

translations.literal: Note: hui “clever” and hui “kind” are treated as interchangeable here.
translations.idiomatic: Editors treat the benevolence and cleverness graphs as variants.

sentences.zh: 二二六一頁九行高明必為偉器按：王先謙謂世說注引續漢書，「高明」上有「長大」二字，似不可少。

translations.literal: Page 2261, line 9: lofty clarity must make a great vessel—note: Wang Xianqian says the Shishuo commentary’s Xu Han shu has “grown tall” before “lofty clarity,” which seems indispensable.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xianqian argues the Xu Han shu gloss adds “grown tall” before “lofty clarity.”

sentences.zh: 二二六二頁一行年十三喪父按：校補引沉銘彝說，謂融父宙卒於桓帝延熹六年正月己未，見孔宙碑，以融卒年計之，則宙卒時，融年十一，非十三也。

translations.literal: Page 2262, line 1: age thirteen when father died—note: the collation cites Shen Mingyi: Rong’s father Zhou died on the jiwei day of the first month of Yanxi 6 of Emperor Huan, per the Kong Zhou stele; reckoning from Rong’s death year, Rong was eleven, not thirteen.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: Kong Rong was eleven, not thirteen, at his father’s death per the stele dating.

sentences.zh: 二二六二頁三行時融年十六按：校補引侯康說，謂詔捕張儉事在建寧二年，融年十七矣。

translations.literal: Page 2262, line 3: at the time Rong was sixteen—note: the collation cites Hou Kang: the warrant for Zhang Jian was in the second Jianning year, when Rong was seventeen.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: at the Zhang Jian incident Rong was seventeen, not sixteen.

sentences.zh: 二二六三頁六行拜中軍候刊誤謂漢官無中軍候，惟有北軍中候耳，明字有脫誤。

translations.literal: Page 2263, line 6: appointed central army commandant—Kanwu says Han offices have no central army commandant, only northern army commandant; clearly a lacuna or error.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: “central army commandant” should be “northern army commandant.”

sentences.zh: 按：校補引錢大昭說，謂魏志崔琰傳注云「累遷北軍中候」此作「中軍候」，誤。

translations.literal: Note: The collation cites Qian Dazhao: the Wei Records, Cui Yan commentary, says “promoted repeatedly to northern army commandant”; here “central army commandant” is wrong.
translations.idiomatic: Qian Dazhao cites the Wei parallel: read northern army commandant.

sentences.zh: 二二六五頁一六行*

translations.literal: Page 2265, line 16: *
translations.idiomatic: Page 2265, line 16: damaged character in the apparatus.

translations.literal: (ji / and)
translations.idiomatic: Alternate reading: ji (“and”).

sentences.zh: **[反]*魯□之侵地刊誤謂案公羊傳本文，「及」當作「反」。

translations.literal: **[fan]* Lu [lacuna] invaded territory—Kanwu says the Gongyang text has ji where this should read fan (“return”).
translations.idiomatic: Collation: per Gongyang, ji should be fan for “restore Lu’s seized lands.”

sentences.zh: 今據改。

translations.literal: Now emended accordingly.
translations.idiomatic: Emended accordingly.

sentences.zh: 按：以下注所引公羊傳文與今本多不合，然意義無大出入。

translations.literal: Note: The Gongyang quotations below differ from modern editions in wording but not greatly in sense.
translations.idiomatic: Later Gongyang quotations diverge slightly from received texts without changing the sense.

sentences.zh: 二二六六頁一０行善否不別按：御覽六四八引續漢書，「不別」作「區別」。

translations.literal: Page 2266, line 10: good and bad not distinguished—note: Imperial Readings 648 citing Xu Han shu writes “distinguish” for “not distinguish.”
translations.idiomatic: Collation: Xu Han shu via Imperial Readings reads “distinguish good from bad.”

sentences.zh: 二二六六頁一三行是下常有千八百紂也按：刊誤謂「是」下少一「天」字。

translations.literal: Page 2266, line 13: below shi there should stand “a thousand eight hundred Zhou”—Kanwu says shi lacks the character tian.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: insert tian below shi to match the source line.

sentences.zh: 二二六八頁七行軍半至刊誤謂案史記，彼文更有他語，故未云「軍半至」，今既節取，不宜長此三字。

translations.literal: Page 2268, line 7: “half the army arrives”—Kanwu says the Records has further sentences before this, so the excerpt should not keep these three characters alone.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: “half the army arrives” is an awkward excerpt from the Records passage.

sentences.zh: 今按：史記作「兵法，百里而趣利者蹶上將，五十里而趣利者軍半至。」

translations.literal: Now checked: the Records reads, “By military doctrine, one who races for gain across a hundred li cripples his upper general; one who races fifty li gets only half his army.”
translations.idiomatic: The Records line runs from “military doctrine” through “half his army.”

sentences.zh: 二二六八頁一０行於是令齊軍曰按：史記無「曰」字。

translations.literal: Page 2268, line 10: thereupon ordered the Qi army yue—note: the Records lack the graph yue (“said”) here.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: Shiji omits the expository 曰 that appears in this text.

sentences.zh: 二二六八頁一０行期日莫見火舉而俱發按：史記「日」作「曰」。

translations.literal: Page 2268, line 10: fix the day at mo, see fire raised and all shoot—note: in the Records the graph ri (“day”) appears as yue (“said”).
translations.idiomatic: Collation: Shiji writes 曰 where this text reads 日 for the word “day.”

sentences.zh: 二二七０頁九行苞茅不入汲本、殿本「苞」作「包」。

translations.literal: Page 2270, line 9: bao mao not presented—Jizhou and Palace write bao without the grass radical.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: bao vs bao for “bundled reeds” in the tribute phrase.

sentences.zh: 按：阮元謂「包茅不入」之「包」，原從艸作「苞」，自石經始去艸頭，後人往往從之。

translations.literal: Note: Ruan Yuan says the original graph for “bundle” in “bundle reeds not presented” was bao with grass; the stone classics dropped the radical and later copyists often followed.
translations.idiomatic: Ruan Yuan traces the grass-headed bao to the stone classics’ simplification.

sentences.zh: 二二七０頁九行包裡束也按：「裡」原斗「裡」，逕改正。

translations.literal: Page 2270, line 9: bao li means wrapped binding—note: the character li in the gloss was mis-copied and is corrected here.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: a duplicated or miswritten li in the gloss is normalized.

sentences.zh: 二二七一頁八行並獻帝子按：校補謂以融所對聖恩敦睦及同產昆弟之說證之，實皆獻帝之諸弟，而靈帝子耳。

translations.literal: Page 2271, line 8: all Emperor Xian’s sons—note: the collation argues from Rong’s reply about imperial grace and full brothers that they were the emperor’s younger brothers, sons of Emperor Ling.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: these princes were Emperor Ling’s sons, not Emperor Xian’s.

sentences.zh: 疑此注本作「並靈帝子」，淺人妄改為「獻」。

translations.literal: Suspect this note originally read “all Emperor Ling’s sons,” shallow editors wrongly changed to Xian.
translations.idiomatic: The gloss likely read “Ling’s sons” before a scribal change to “Xian.”

sentences.zh: 二二七二頁一０行單于徙北海上按：張森楷校勘記謂「徙」下疑有「之」字。

translations.literal: Page 2272, line 10: the Chanyu moved to the northern sea—note: Zhang Senkai’s collation suspects zhi (“to”) is missing after “moved.”
translations.idiomatic: Collation: possibly insert zhi after “moved” for “moved to the sea.”

sentences.zh: 二二七四頁二行獻帝嘗時見慮按：刊誤謂案文「時」當作「特」。

translations.literal: Page 2274, line 2: Emperor Xian once shi saw Lu—Kanwu says shi should read te (“specially”).
translations.idiomatic: Collation: read te for shi—“specially summoned Lu.”

sentences.zh: 二二七四頁一五行令宗欽馮愔守栒邑按：集解引周壽昌說，謂案鄧禹傳，「宗欽」作「宗歆」。

translations.literal: Page 2274, line 15: ordered Zong Qin and Feng Yin to hold Xunyi—note: the collected commentary cites Zhou Shouchang: in Deng Yu’s biography “Zong Qin” is Zong Xin.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: Zong Qin should be Zong Xin per Deng Yu’s biography.

sentences.zh: 二二七六頁一三行令信出跨下汲本、殿本「跨」作「胯」。

translations.literal: Page 2276, line 13: ordered Xin to pass under the crotch—Jizhou and Palace write kua for kua.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: kua / kua variant for “between the legs.”

sentences.zh: 按：跨胯同。

translations.literal: Note: kua and kua are the same.
translations.idiomatic: The two graphs are equivalent.

sentences.zh: 二二七七頁一行酒酸*

translations.literal: Page 2277, line 1: sour wine*
translations.idiomatic: Page 2277, line 1: damaged particle after “sour wine.”

translations.literal: (zhe / one who)
translations.idiomatic: Supplied reading: zhe (“one who”).

sentences.zh: *據今本韓非子刪。

translations.literal: *Deleted per the received Han Feizi.
translations.idiomatic: The particle is absent in the modern Han Feizi.

sentences.zh: 二二七七頁一行*

translations.literal: Page 2277, line 1: *
translations.idiomatic: Page 2277, line 1: lacuna in the parable.

sentences.zh: (二人)

translations.literal: (two men)
translations.idiomatic: Gloss supplies “two men.”

sentences.zh: **[倩]*曰汝狗猛耶據今本韓非子改。

translations.literal: **[qian]* says your dog is fierce ye—emended per the modern Han Feizi.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: the Han Feizi wording for the neighbor’s question is adopted.

sentences.zh: 二二七七頁五行*[曰然谷]*將□之按：韓非子作「曰然谷將棄之」，此脫「曰然谷」三字，今據補。

translations.literal: Page 2277, line 5: *[yue ran gu]* will [lacuna] it—note: Han Feizi reads “yue ran gu will abandon it”; this text lacks yue ran gu and is supplied.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: three characters missing before “will abandon,” restored from Han Feizi.

sentences.zh: 二二七八頁八行譬如寄物燦中按：殿本「燦」作「瓶」。

translations.literal: Page 2278, line 8: like putting a thing in a can—note: the Palace edition writes ping for can.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: can / ping (“jar”) variant.

sentences.zh: 二二七九頁二行燦缶也按：沈家本謂按說文，缾，□也，瓶缾或從□。

translations.literal: Page 2279, line 2: can is a fou—note: Shen Jiaben says the Shuowen has ping, jar, ping or from fou.
translations.idiomatic: Shen Jiaben cites Shuowen parallels for ping as jar.

sentences.zh: 此注言缶也，疑傳寫奪爛其半耳。

translations.literal: This gloss says fou; suspect copying stripped half the character.
translations.idiomatic: The gloss probably meant fou but was damaged in transmission.

sentences.zh: 「瓶」字本或作「燦」者誤，說文無燦字也。

translations.literal: Where ping is written can is wrong; Shuowen has no can graph.
translations.idiomatic: Ping miswritten as can has no Shuowen authority.

sentences.zh: 二二八０頁三行豈有員□委屈可以每其生哉汲本「有員」作「其負」。

translations.literal: Page 2280, line 3: how can there be round [lacuna] and self-bending to prolong life—Jizhou reads “its burden” for “have round.”
translations.idiomatic: Collation: Jizhou reads qi fu instead of you yuan.

sentences.zh: 校補謂負，恃也，恃員道以為委屈也。

translations.literal: The collation supplement says fu means rely, relying on the round way as self-bending.
translations.idiomatic: One editor glosses fu as “rely on” the constant way.

sentences.zh: □可通員，作「員□」於義為窒，似誤。

translations.literal: [lacuna] can interchange with yuan; writing “yuan[lacuna]” makes awkward sense and seems wrong.
translations.idiomatic: Another argues the lacunae break the parallel couplet.

sentences.zh: 今按：員□委屈，相對成文，古人自有復語耳，作「負」者鬥，校補說非。

translations.literal: Now checked: yuan[lacuna] and qu qu form a parallel; ancients used such double phrasing; writing fu is corruption, and the supplement is wrong.
translations.idiomatic: The editor defends the parallel reading and rejects the fu emendation.

sentences.zh: 二二八一頁一一行亢父*[縣]*屬梁國據汲本、殿本補。

translations.literal: Page 2281, line 11: Kangfu *[county]* belongs to Liang—supplied per Jizhou and Palace.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: add “county” after Kangfu per the editions.

sentences.zh: 二二八一頁一五行彧明有意數按：刊誤謂「明」上當有一「聰」字。

translations.literal: Page 2281, line 15: Yu ming you yi shu—Kanwu says cong should stand before ming.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: insert cong before ming—“keenly perceptive in counsel.”

sentences.zh: 二二八二頁一行明年又為操鎮東司馬按：集解引錢大昕說，謂此初平二年之明年也。

translations.literal: Page 2282, line 1: the next year again served Cao as eastern garrison marshal—note: collected commentary cites Qian Daxin: this is the year after the second Chuping.
translations.idiomatic: Qian Daxin dates the line to the year after Chuping 2.

sentences.zh: 據魏志，操為鎮東將軍在建安元年，則初平三年安得便稱鎮東司馬乎？

translations.literal: According to the Wei Records, Cao became eastern garrison general in the first Jian’an year, so how could the third Chuping year already call him eastern garrison marshal?
translations.idiomatic: Cao’s eastern garrison title belongs to Jian’an 1, not Chuping 3.

sentences.zh: 魏志彧傳本雲明年太祖領兗州牧，後為鎮東將軍，常以司馬從。

translations.literal: The Wei Records, Yu’s biography, says the next year the Grand Progenitor took Yanzhou shepherd, later became eastern garrison general, and always had a marshal attend him.
translations.idiomatic: The Wei text orders Yanzhou first, then the eastern garrison appointment.

sentences.zh: 然則領兗州在此年，而除鎮東不在此年也。

translations.literal: Thus taking Yanzhou falls in this year, but appointment as eastern garrison general is not this year.
translations.idiomatic: He took Yanzhou this year; the eastern garrison rank came later.

sentences.zh: 范史刪去領兗州句，遂誤以鎮東司馬為是年事矣。

translations.literal: Fan Ye’s history deleted the Yanzhou clause, wrongly making eastern garrison marshal this year’s event.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Ye’s omission of Yanzhou skews the chronology.

sentences.zh: 二二八二頁六行宜亟供軍實按：集解引惠棟說，謂「實」魏志作「食」。

translations.literal: Page 2282, line 6: should urgently supply army shi—note: collected commentary cites Hui Dong: shi in the Wei Records reads shi (“food”).
translations.idiomatic: Collation: Wei parallel reads “food” not “matériel.”

sentences.zh: 二二八三頁六行而將軍之關河也按：集解引錢大昕說，謂「關河」當依魏志彧傳作「關中河內」，蓋上言高祖保關中，光武據河內，皆深根固本，以制天下，故以兗州比關中、河內。

translations.literal: Page 2283, line 6: and the general’s guan he—note: collected commentary cites Qian Daxin: guan he should follow the Wei Records, Yu’s biography, as “Guanzhong and Henei,” since above Gaozu held Guanzhong, Guangwu held Henei—both deep roots to control the empire—so Yanzhou is compared to Guanzhong and Henei.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: read “Guanzhong and Henei,” not the compressed guan he.

sentences.zh: 范史刪去二字，未當。

translations.literal: Fan Ye’s history deleted two characters; that is not apt.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Ye’s shortening loses the geographical parallel.

sentences.zh: 二二八三頁一五行東郡守按：刊誤謂案文少一「太」字。

translations.literal: Page 2283, line 15: governor of Dong commandery—Kanwu says the text lacks tai (“grand”).
translations.idiomatic: Collation: supply tai—“grand administrator.”

sentences.zh: 二二八六頁八行*[書]*與彧議據殿本補。

translations.literal: Page 2286, line 8: *[shu]* consulted Yu—supplied per Palace edition.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: add shu (“letter”) before consulting Yu.

sentences.zh: 按：下文云「彧報曰」，則此當有「書」字。

translations.literal: Note: Below it says “Yu replied,” so there should be a “letter” here.
translations.idiomatic: The reply implies a prior written inquiry.

sentences.zh: 二二八九頁二行各規利人百其勇也按：「各」原斗「名」，逕改正。

translations.literal: Page 2289, line 2: each seeks profit, men redouble their courage—note: ge was corrupted to ming; corrected directly.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: ge for ming—“each man” not “fame.”

sentences.zh: 二二八九頁七行發[縱]指示功人也據汲本補。

translations.literal: Page 2289, line 7: fa [zong] zhi shi, the meritorious man—supplied per Jizhou edition.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: insert zong in fa zong zhi shi per Jizhou.

sentences.zh: 二二九０頁五行國之*

translations.literal: Page 2290, line 5: the state’s *
translations.idiomatic: Page 2290, line 5: lacuna in “pillar of the state.”

translations.literal: (wang / hope)
translations.idiomatic: Alternate reading: wang (“hope”).

sentences.zh: **[重]*臣據汲本、殿本改。

translations.literal: **[zhong]* minister—emended per Jizhou and Palace.
translations.idiomatic: Collation: read zhong chen (“weighty minister”) per the editions.
